questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.text: An instructor reviews the AHA age definitions used in the BLS pediatric section. Which range correctly describes an 'infant' for BLS purposes, excluding the newly born?

answers.text: From age 1 through puberty
Younger than 1 year
Birth to age 5
Younger than 6 months only

explanations.a: From 1 year to puberty defines a child, not an infant.
explanations.b: AHA Part 1 defines an infant as someone younger than 1 year, excluding newly born infants in the delivery room.
explanations.c: Birth-to-5 spans both infant and child categories and is not the AHA infant definition.
explanations.d: The infant category extends through the first year of life, not just the first 6 months.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.text: You are caring for a 13-year-old who has visible chest hair and is in cardiac arrest. According to AHA Part 1, which BLS approach should you use?

answers.text: Use pediatric BLS because of chronologic age
Use neonatal resuscitation guidelines
Treat as an adult because there are signs of puberty
Wait for parental consent before any care

explanations.a: AHA defines the adult range as starting at puberty, regardless of chronologic age below 18.
explanations.b: Neonatal guidelines apply to the newly born in the delivery room, not adolescents.
explanations.c: AHA Part 1 lists chest or underarm hair on males and any breast development on females as signs of puberty, after which BLS treats the patient as an adult.
explanations.d: Cardiac arrest requires immediate care; consent is implied in life-threatening emergencies.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.text: AHA Part 6 explains why pediatric CPR includes both compressions and breaths even when adult Hands-Only CPR can be effective. Which physiologic reason does the manual cite?

answers.text: Children always have shorter resuscitation times than adults
Pediatric cardiac arrests are commonly due to respiratory causes, so blood oxygen content is already low before arrest
Children's hearts cannot generate any electrical activity
Compression-only CPR is unsafe for any age group

explanations.a: Resuscitation duration is not the AHA-cited rationale for breaths in pediatric CPR.
explanations.b: AHA Part 6 explains that infant and child arrests are commonly due to respiratory causes, so oxygen content is reduced before arrest and compressions alone do not deliver oxygenated blood as effectively as compressions plus breaths.
explanations.c: Children's hearts can have shockable rhythms; the rationale is about oxygen content, not electrical activity.
explanations.d: Compression-only CPR is recommended for untrained adult lay rescuers; it is not unsafe at any age, just suboptimal for pediatrics.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.text: Which range does AHA Part 1 use to define a 'child' for BLS purposes?

answers.text: From age 6 to age 12 only
From birth to age 2
From 1 year of age to puberty
Anyone younger than 18 regardless of physical development

explanations.a: Restricting to age 6-12 excludes younger children covered by pediatric BLS.
explanations.b: Birth to age 2 includes infants and only the youngest children, not the full child range.
explanations.c: AHA Part 1 defines a child as anyone from 1 year of age to the onset of puberty.
explanations.d: Adolescents who have reached puberty are treated as adults under BLS, not as children.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.text: You are alone with an unresponsive 8-month-old whose collapse you did not witness, and you have no mobile device. According to the pediatric single-rescuer algorithm, what should you do before leaving to activate EMS?

answers.text: Leave immediately to call for help
Wait until breathing returns spontaneously
Provide breaths only and never give compressions
Perform 5 cycles or about 2 minutes of CPR first

explanations.a: Leaving an unwitnessed pediatric victim before any CPR omits the most important early intervention for a respiratory cause.
explanations.b: Waiting for spontaneous breathing during cardiac arrest is not an algorithm step and only delays care.
explanations.c: Compressions are essential; pediatric CPR requires both compressions and breaths.
explanations.d: AHA Part 6 directs the lone rescuer at an unwitnessed pediatric collapse without a mobile device to perform 5 cycles or about 2 minutes of CPR before leaving to activate EMS and get an AED.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.text: You are alone with a 5-year-old you saw suddenly collapse, and no mobile device is available. According to the AHA pediatric single-rescuer sequence, what is the correct action?

answers.text: Stay at the child's side and wait for someone to find you
Provide 30 minutes of CPR before any activation
Leave the child to activate EMS and get an AED, then return to perform CPR
Continue checking responsiveness every minute and do nothing else

explanations.a: Doing nothing while waiting wastes minutes during which the brain is being deprived of oxygen.
explanations.b: An indefinitely long delay before activation contradicts the witnessed-collapse rule and lowers survival.
explanations.c: AHA Part 6 directs a lone rescuer who witnessed a child's sudden collapse to leave to activate EMS and get an AED, then return to perform CPR.
explanations.d: Repeated responsiveness checks without action do not address cardiac arrest.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.text: An infant lies motionless on a kitchen floor. According to Step 1 of the pediatric BLS single-rescuer sequence, what is the rescuer's very first action?

answers.text: Apply AED pads before reaching the infant
Begin chest compressions immediately
Verify that the scene is safe for the rescuer and the infant
Wait for parents to arrive before any action

explanations.a: AED pads can only be placed after the rescuer is at the child's side with the AED ready.
explanations.b: Compressions cannot be provided until the rescuer has reached the child and confirmed cardiac arrest.
explanations.c: AHA Part 6 makes Step 1 of the pediatric sequence an explicit scene safety verification for the rescuer and the infant.
explanations.d: Waiting for parents wastes minutes when a child's brain is failing.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.text: When you begin CPR alone on an unresponsive child or infant in cardiac arrest, what compression-to-ventilation ratio does AHA Part 6 specify for a single rescuer?

answers.text: 5 compressions to 1 breath
15 compressions to 2 breaths
30 compressions to 2 breaths
Continuous compressions with no breaths

explanations.a: 5:1 is not part of any current AHA recommendation.
explanations.b: The 15:2 ratio applies when 2 or more rescuers are providing CPR to a child or infant, not when a single rescuer is alone.
explanations.c: AHA Part 6 says the compression-to-ventilation ratio for single rescuers is 30:2 in adults, children, and infants.
explanations.d: Pediatric CPR includes breaths because the arrest is most often respiratory in origin; continuous compressions without breaths is not the recommendation.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.text: While performing CPR alone on a child, you finally retrieve the AED. AHA Part 6 directs you to do what with the device?

answers.text: Use it only if the child does not regain a pulse after 10 minutes
Wait until 5 full cycles of CPR are completed before turning it on
Use the AED as soon as it is available
Avoid using an AED on a child of any age

explanations.a: Survival drops with every minute of arrest; waiting 10 minutes is not part of the algorithm.
explanations.b: Delaying AED use after retrieval contradicts the principle of early defibrillation.
explanations.c: AHA Part 6 directs rescuers to use the AED/defibrillator as soon as it is available during pediatric resuscitation.
explanations.d: AEDs are absolutely indicated for children; pediatric pads or attenuators are used when available.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.text: You and a coworker simultaneously discover an unresponsive infant. According to the pediatric BLS multirescuer sequence, how should the two of you divide the initial tasks?

answers.text: Both rescuers leave to call for help, then return
The first rescuer remains with the infant while the second activates EMS and retrieves the AED
Both rescuers stand back and wait for paramedics
The second rescuer alone performs all initial assessment and care

explanations.a: Both rescuers leaving the infant abandons the patient; one must stay to provide care.
explanations.b: AHA Part 6 explicitly directs the first rescuer to remain with the infant or child while the second rescuer activates EMS and retrieves the AED.
explanations.c: Standing back during pediatric arrest is never the multirescuer plan.
explanations.d: Splitting tasks effectively means both rescuers are working — one stays and provides care while the other activates and retrieves equipment.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.text: You begin pediatric CPR alone using a 30:2 ratio. When the second rescuer returns, AHA Part 6 directs the team to switch to which compression-to-ventilation ratio?

answers.text: Continue at 30:2 until ALS arrives
Switch to continuous compressions with no breaths
Switch to 15 compressions to 2 breaths
Switch to 50 compressions to 1 breath

explanations.a: Continuing 30:2 with two rescuers misses the AHA-recommended pediatric ratio change.
explanations.b: Continuous compressions without breaths is for adults with an advanced airway, not pediatric two-rescuer BLS.
explanations.c: AHA Part 6 specifies 15:2 when 2 or more rescuers are working on an infant or child, prioritizing ventilation because pediatric arrests are commonly respiratory in origin.
explanations.d: 50:1 is not part of any current AHA recommendation.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.text: Step 2 of the pediatric multirescuer sequence directs the first rescuer to check responsiveness. Which technique is correct for a child?

answers.text: Pinch the cheek silently
Slap the back firmly
Lift the eyelids and check pupils
Tap the child's shoulders and shout, 'Hey! Are you OK? Are you OK?'

explanations.a: Cheek pinching is not the AHA-recommended responsiveness check.
explanations.b: Back slaps are an FBAO maneuver for choking infants, not a responsiveness check.
explanations.c: Pupil checks are not part of the BLS responsiveness assessment.
explanations.d: AHA Part 6 directs the rescuer to tap the child's shoulders and shout, 'Hey! Are you OK? Are you OK?' to assess responsiveness.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.text: Per AHA Part 6, when the responsiveness check during the multirescuer pediatric sequence is being performed on an infant, where should the rescuer tap?

answers.text: Both shoulders, the same as for an adult
The infant's heel
The forehead between the eyes
The abdomen near the navel

explanations.a: Shoulder tapping is for adults and children, not infants.
explanations.b: AHA Part 6 directs rescuers to tap the infant's heel and shout to check responsiveness.
explanations.c: Forehead tapping is not the recommended infant assessment site.
explanations.d: Abdominal tapping is not part of any AHA responsiveness check.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.text: During pediatric resuscitation, the AED prompts that a shockable rhythm is detected. According to the multirescuer sequence, what should the team do after delivering the shock?

answers.text: Pause for 5 minutes to allow recovery
Check the pulse for at least 60 seconds before resuming care
Stop CPR until the child shows spontaneous movement
Immediately resume CPR for 2 minutes until the AED prompts another rhythm check

explanations.a: A 5-minute pause would abandon the resuscitation entirely during a critical window.
explanations.b: Sixty-second post-shock pulse checks contradict AHA timing and delay restart of compressions.
explanations.c: Stopping CPR after a shock is the opposite of the algorithm direction; immediate resumption maintains perfusion.
explanations.d: AHA Part 6 directs the team to immediately resume CPR for 2 minutes after a shock, until the AED prompts another rhythm check.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.text: AHA Part 6 gives a specific physiologic reason for using 15:2 instead of 30:2 when 2 rescuers work on a child or infant. What is that reason?

answers.text: It allows the AED to charge faster
It reduces the rescuer's fatigue without affecting the patient
It prioritizes ventilation because pediatric arrests are commonly due to respiratory causes
It is required by state law in most U.S. jurisdictions

explanations.a: AED charging speed is independent of compression-to-ventilation ratio.
explanations.b: Rescuer fatigue is real but is not the AHA rationale for the ratio change.
explanations.c: AHA Part 6 explains that 15:2 prioritizes ventilation because pediatric arrests are commonly due to respiratory causes.
explanations.d: AHA guidelines drive the ratio choice rather than state law.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.text: An infant has abnormal breathing but a definite pulse is felt. According to AHA Part 6 Step 3b, what breath rate should the rescuer provide?

answers.text: 1 breath every 6 seconds, or 10 breaths per minute
1 breath every 2 to 3 seconds, or 20 to 30 breaths per minute
1 breath every 10 seconds, or 6 breaths per minute
No breaths until cardiac arrest is confirmed

explanations.a: Ten breaths per minute is the adult rate after advanced airway placement, not the pediatric rate for respiratory failure.
explanations.b: AHA Part 6 Step 3b specifies 1 breath every 2 to 3 seconds, or 20 to 30 breaths per minute, when an infant or child has abnormal breathing but a pulse.
explanations.c: Six breaths per minute is below the AHA pediatric range for support of ventilation.
explanations.d: Withholding breaths until full arrest contradicts the algorithm; respiratory failure with a pulse calls for immediate ventilation.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.text: A pediatric advanced airway is placed during a child's resuscitation. AHA's high-quality CPR table specifies which compression and ventilation strategy after advanced airway placement?

answers.text: Stop ventilations once the airway is placed
Continuous compressions at 60 per minute and 1 breath every 2 seconds
Pause compressions to give 2 breaths every 30 compressions
Continuous compressions at 100 to 120 per minute and 1 breath every 2 to 3 seconds

explanations.a: Ventilations remain essential after an advanced airway, just asynchronous with compressions.
explanations.b: 60 per minute is below the AHA-specified compression rate.
explanations.c: Pausing compressions for breaths defeats the purpose of an advanced airway.
explanations.d: AHA's high-quality CPR table for children/infants with an advanced airway calls for continuous compressions at 100 to 120 per minute with 1 breath every 2 to 3 seconds — 20 to 30 breaths per minute.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.text: How long does approximately 5 cycles of single-rescuer 30:2 pediatric CPR take, according to the AHA Part 6 reference often used in algorithm steps?

answers.text: About 30 minutes
About 30 seconds
About 10 minutes
About 2 minutes

explanations.a: Thirty minutes overstates the time required for 5 cycles by an order of magnitude.
explanations.b: Thirty seconds is far too short for 5 full 30:2 cycles.
explanations.c: Ten minutes does not match the actual rate of 30:2 cycles at 100 to 120 compressions per minute.
explanations.d: AHA Part 6 references about 2 minutes for 5 cycles of 30:2 CPR; that is the duration used in the lone-rescuer-unwitnessed-collapse step.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.keyword: ratio compares adult child infant single
questions.text: An instructor compares single-rescuer compression-to-ventilation ratios across adults, children, and infants. Which statement is consistent with AHA Part 6?

answers.text: Adults are 30:2; children are 50:2; infants are 15:2
Adults are 30:2; children and infants are 30:2 as well for a single rescuer
Adults are 15:2; children are 15:2; infants are 5:1
Adults are continuous; children are continuous; infants are 30:2

explanations.a: Children are not 50:2 in any AHA configuration; the single-rescuer ratio is the same as adults.
explanations.b: AHA Part 6 says the single-rescuer compression-to-ventilation ratio is the same — 30:2 — in adults, children, and infants.
explanations.c: Adults at 15:2 contradicts AHA guidance; the adult ratio is 30:2 with one or two rescuers.
explanations.d: Continuous compressions without breaths apply only after advanced airway placement, not as the default ratio at any age.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.text: When performing chest compressions on an infant in cardiac arrest, what depth does AHA Part 6 specify?

answers.text: Less than half an inch to avoid injury
At least 2 inches (5 cm) regardless of body size
At least 3 inches (7.5 cm)
At least one third the AP diameter of the chest, approximately 1 1/2 inches (4 cm)

explanations.a: Compressing less than half an inch fails to generate adequate cardiac output.
explanations.b: Two inches is the adult depth, not the infant depth, and would be excessive on an infant chest.
explanations.c: Three inches is far beyond the AHA-specified infant depth and would risk serious injury.
explanations.d: AHA Part 6 specifies infant compressions of at least one third the AP diameter of the chest, approximately 1 1/2 inches or 4 cm.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.text: When performing chest compressions on a 6-year-old in cardiac arrest, what depth does AHA Part 6 specify?

answers.text: At least 1 inch (2.5 cm)
At least one third the AP diameter of the chest, approximately 2 inches (5 cm)
At least 4 inches (10 cm)
Exactly 1 1/2 inches (4 cm), the same as an infant

explanations.a: One inch falls below the AHA-specified child depth and would not generate adequate output.
explanations.b: AHA Part 6 specifies child compressions of at least one third the AP diameter of the chest, approximately 2 inches or 5 cm.
explanations.c: Four inches is far beyond the AHA-specified child depth.
explanations.d: Children require deeper compressions than infants because their chests are larger.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.text: AHA Part 6 expresses pediatric compression depth as 'at least one third the AP diameter' of the chest. Why use a fraction rather than a fixed measurement for children and infants?

answers.text: It is the same fraction used for adult chests
It prevents the rescuer from compressing too fast
It removes the need to use compressions at all
It accommodates the wide range of pediatric body sizes from infant to adolescent

explanations.a: Adult depth is given as a fixed minimum, not as a fraction, because adult chest size is more uniform.
explanations.b: Compression rate is a separate parameter not tied to depth fractions.
explanations.c: Pediatric CPR absolutely includes compressions; the fraction simply scales depth.
explanations.d: Pediatric body size varies dramatically across ages, so AHA expresses depth as a fraction of the chest diameter that scales with the patient.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.text: Which statement about chest compression rate across age groups is consistent with AHA Part 6?

answers.text: Infants need 60 to 80 per minute because they are small
Children need 80 to 100 per minute
Adults need 140 to 160 per minute
The rate is the same — 100 to 120 per minute — for all people in cardiac arrest

explanations.a: Infants receive the same rate as adults; only the depth and hand technique differ.
explanations.b: Children are also compressed at 100 to 120 per minute, not at a slower pediatric-specific rate.
explanations.c: 140 to 160 exceeds the recommended adult range.
explanations.d: AHA Part 6 calls 100 to 120 per minute the universal rate for compressions in all people who experience cardiac arrest.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.text: You are alone with an infant in cardiac arrest. Which compression technique does AHA Part 6 specifically recommend for a single rescuer when you cannot encircle the chest?

answers.text: Use the heel of one hand on the lower half of the sternum
Use both fists side by side on the upper sternum
Press laterally on the ribs from one side
Use only the fingertips of one hand

explanations.a: AHA Part 6 says if the rescuer cannot encircle the chest, the recommended technique is to compress with the heel of one hand on the lower half of the sternum.
explanations.b: Two fists on the upper sternum is not a recognized infant technique.
explanations.c: Lateral pressure on the ribs does not produce effective central chest compression.
explanations.d: Fingertip-only compression is not the AHA technique; the heel of one hand is preferred when 2-thumb technique is not feasible.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.text: Two rescuers are providing pediatric CPR to an infant. AHA Part 6 specifies which compression technique is preferred when 2 rescuers are available?

answers.text: The 2 thumb-encircling hands technique
The single fingertip technique
The fist on the abdomen technique
The two-handed adult technique on infants

explanations.a: AHA Part 6 describes the 2 thumb-encircling hands technique with the rescuer's thumbs side by side on the lower half of the sternum and the fingers encircling the chest to support the back, used when 2 rescuers are available.
explanations.b: Single fingertip technique is not a recognized AHA infant compression method.
explanations.c: Compressing the abdomen does not generate cardiac output and is not an AHA technique.
explanations.d: Two-handed adult technique is too forceful for an infant chest and is not recommended.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.text: AHA Part 6 says compressions on a child can be performed with one or two hands depending on the situation. What is the principle that guides the choice?

answers.text: Use whichever method achieves at least one third AP-diameter depth, approximately 2 inches (5 cm)
Always use two hands on every child regardless of size
Always use one hand even on adolescents
Use only the heel of one hand for children over 8 years

explanations.a: AHA Part 6 says whether one or two hands is used, the rescuer compresses at least one third the AP diameter of the chest, approximately 2 inches or 5 cm; the choice is driven by the child's size and the rescuer's strength.
explanations.b: Two hands are not always required; small children may receive adequate depth with one.
explanations.c: Adolescents who reach puberty are treated as adults and compressed with two hands.
explanations.d: AHA does not restrict children over 8 to one-handed compressions; either technique can be used as long as adequate depth is achieved.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.text: When using the 2 thumb-encircling hands technique on an infant, where does AHA Part 6 instruct the rescuer to position the thumbs?

answers.text: Side by side in the center of the chest, on the lower half of the sternum
On the upper sternum just below the clavicles
Directly over the xiphoid process
On the side of the chest along the ribs

explanations.a: AHA Part 6 instructs that thumbs go side by side in the center of the chest on the lower half of the sternum, with the hands encircling and supporting the back.
explanations.b: Upper sternum placement near the clavicles produces poor cardiac output.
explanations.c: Pressing directly on the xiphoid risks fracturing it and injuring underlying organs.
explanations.d: Lateral rib placement is not AHA technique and will not generate effective compression.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.text: Before starting compressions on an infant, AHA Part 6 instructs the rescuer to place the infant on a particular surface. Which surface is correct?

answers.text: A firm, flat surface
A soft pillow to cushion the back
The rescuer's lap if no firm surface is available
An inclined surface at 45 degrees

explanations.a: AHA Part 6 explicitly directs the rescuer to place the infant on a firm, flat surface so compression force translates into actual chest depression.
explanations.b: A soft pillow absorbs compression force and reduces real chest depression even when the rescuer compresses the right amount.
explanations.c: Compressing on a lap is not an AHA-recommended substitute for a firm flat surface.
explanations.d: An inclined surface complicates compression mechanics and is not part of AHA technique.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.text: When opening the airway of an infant, AHA Part 6 emphasizes a specific neck position to maximize an open airway. Which position is described?

answers.text: Hyperextended with the chin pointing upward toward the ceiling
Neutral or sniffing position so the external ear canal is level with the top of the shoulder
Flexed forward with the chin against the chest
Rotated 90 degrees to one side

explanations.a: Hyperextending an infant's neck can collapse the soft trachea and block the airway.
explanations.b: AHA Part 6 critical concept directs the rescuer to keep the infant's neck in neutral or sniffing position so the external ear canal is level with the top of the infant's shoulder.
explanations.c: Forward neck flexion closes rather than opens the airway.
explanations.d: Rotating the head 90 degrees to one side does not open the airway.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.text: A second rescuer arrives with a bag-mask device for a pediatric resuscitation. According to AHA Part 6, which technique does the rescuer use to hold the mask against the infant's or child's face?

answers.text: The E-C clamp technique with one hand
Tape the mask to the cheeks
Pinch the mask edges between two fingers only
Hold the mask loosely above the face

explanations.a: AHA Part 6 instructs use of the E-C clamp technique to hold the mask against the face while lifting the jaw, creating a seal between the face and the mask.
explanations.b: Taping the mask is not an AHA-recommended technique and would not produce a reliable seal.
explanations.c: Pinching the edges is unreliable and leaks air around the seal.
explanations.d: Holding the mask above the face does not create a seal at all.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.text: AHA Part 6 instructs the rescuer to choose a mask of appropriate size when providing bag-mask ventilation to an infant or child. Which description matches the criteria the manual specifies?

answers.text: The mask must cover only the mouth, leaving the nose uncovered
The mask must cover the eyes for full facial coverage
The mask must extend several inches below the chin
The mask must cover the mouth and nose completely without covering the eyes or extending below the bottom edge of the chin

explanations.a: Leaving the nose uncovered allows air to leak and prevents an effective seal.
explanations.b: Covering the eyes is harmful and not part of mask sizing.
explanations.c: A mask that extends below the chin cannot seal properly.
explanations.d: AHA Part 6 specifies the mask must cover the mouth and nose completely without covering the eyes or extending below the bottom edge of the chin.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.text: When providing bag-mask ventilation to an infant or small child, AHA Part 6 cautions about volume and force. Which description matches the manual's guidance?

answers.text: Use the same volume as for adults; the child needs full inflation
Use less volume and force than for adults, just enough to see the chest rise
Squeeze the bag fully and quickly to overcome airway resistance
Provide as much volume as possible to flush carbon dioxide

explanations.a: Adult-volume breaths in an infant overinflate the lungs and risk barotrauma.
explanations.b: AHA Part 6 says delivering ventilations to infants or small children requires less volume and force than for adults, while still ensuring enough air to see the chest rise.
explanations.c: Forceful, rapid squeezing causes gastric inflation and lung trauma.
explanations.d: Maximum-volume breaths cause hyperinflation and reduce cardiac output rather than improving CO2 clearance.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.keyword: HR less than 60 poor perfusion start CPR
questions.text: You are providing breaths to a child in respiratory failure. On reassessment, the heart rate is 50 per minute with cool, mottled extremities and continued declining responsiveness despite oxygenation and ventilation. What does the AHA pediatric BLS algorithm direct you to do next?

answers.text: Continue ventilations only and do not start chest compressions
Wait two more minutes before any change in care
Begin CPR with chest compressions and ventilations
Stop all care and reassess after the parents arrive

explanations.a: Ventilations alone are insufficient when heart rate is under 60 with signs of poor perfusion despite oxygenation.
explanations.b: Waiting worsens outcome; the algorithm requires an immediate change in care at this threshold.
explanations.c: AHA Part 6 directs the rescuer to start CPR when a child's heart rate is under 60 with signs of poor perfusion despite oxygenation and ventilation.
explanations.d: Stopping care to wait for family is never the correct algorithm action during a deteriorating pediatric resuscitation.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.text: AHA Part 6 expresses the pediatric bradycardia threshold in terms a rescuer can count at the bedside. Which equivalent does the manual provide?

answers.text: Heart rate less than 60 per minute, equal to fewer than 6 beats in 10 seconds
Heart rate less than 100 per minute, equal to fewer than 10 beats in 10 seconds
Heart rate less than 30 per minute, equal to fewer than 3 beats in 10 seconds
Heart rate less than 80 per minute, equal to fewer than 8 beats in 10 seconds

explanations.a: AHA Part 6 expresses the bradycardia trigger as fewer than 60 per minute, equal to fewer than 6 beats in 10 seconds.
explanations.b: 100 per minute is well above the bradycardia threshold the algorithm uses.
explanations.c: 30 per minute is far below the threshold and would describe near-asystole.
explanations.d: 80 per minute is above the AHA-defined threshold of 60.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.text: An 8-year-old in cardiac arrest receives high-quality CPR while a coworker fetches the AED. According to the AHA pediatric BLS sequence, when should the AED be applied?

answers.text: Use it as soon as it is available
Wait until the child has been in arrest for 10 minutes
Apply it only if the child does not have a pulse after 5 minutes
Avoid using an AED on any child

explanations.a: AHA Part 6 directs the team to use the AED/defibrillator as soon as it is available during pediatric resuscitation.
explanations.b: A 10-minute delay before defibrillation lowers survival; early defibrillation is the goal.
explanations.c: Waiting 5 minutes contradicts the principle of early defibrillation.
explanations.d: AEDs are absolutely indicated for children; pediatric pads or attenuators are used when available.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.text: During pediatric resuscitation of an infant, the AED detects a shockable rhythm. According to the algorithm, what is the appropriate next action?

answers.text: Give 1 shock and immediately resume CPR for 2 minutes
Give 3 stacked shocks before resuming CPR
Continue CPR for 5 minutes before any shock
Wait for ALS personnel to authorize the shock

explanations.a: AHA Part 6 directs the team to give 1 shock and immediately resume CPR for 2 minutes when the AED detects a shockable rhythm.
explanations.b: Stacked shocks are not part of current AHA BLS guidance.
explanations.c: Continuing CPR without delivering an indicated shock violates the algorithm and lowers survival.
explanations.d: AHA BLS does not require ALS authorization to deliver an AED shock; the AED itself analyzes and prompts.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.text: A daycare worker asks how AHA categorizes a 9-month-old patient. According to AHA Part 6, this child is classified as which patient type for BLS purposes?

answers.text: Infant — defined as under 1 year of age (excluding newborns at the moment of delivery)
Newborn — applies to any patient under 1 year of age
Child — applies to anyone weighing under 25 kg
Adolescent — used because the child can sit unsupported

explanations.a: AHA Part 6: infant is under 1 year of age, excluding newborns at the time of birth — a 9-month-old is an infant.
explanations.b: Newborn applies only at the time of delivery; after delivery, BLS terminology is "infant."
explanations.c: Age categorization in BLS is by age and pubertal status, not weight.
explanations.d: Adolescent is not a separate BLS category; child applies through puberty.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.text: An ED physician explains why high-quality ventilation is especially important during pediatric resuscitation. According to AHA Part 6, what is the typical mechanism leading to pediatric cardiac arrest that drives this emphasis?

answers.text: Pediatric arrests are typically caused by sudden ventricular fibrillation as in adults
Most pediatric arrests result from progressive respiratory failure or shock leading to hypoxia and acidosis, so oxygen delivery via effective ventilation is central to resuscitation
Pediatric arrests are most commonly caused by congenital heart block requiring pacing
Pediatric arrests are unrelated to oxygenation, so chest compressions alone are sufficient

explanations.a: Adult arrests are commonly VF/pulseless VT; pediatric arrests usually are not.
explanations.b: AHA Part 6: pediatric arrest is most often the end result of respiratory failure or shock, making airway and ventilation central to pediatric resuscitation.
explanations.c: Heart block as a primary cause of arrest is rare in children.
explanations.d: Effective ventilation and compressions together — not compressions alone — produce best outcomes in pediatric arrest.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.text: A single lay rescuer is alone with a child who has just collapsed. According to AHA Part 6 single-rescuer pediatric BLS, what should the rescuer do FIRST after confirming unresponsiveness and absent/abnormal breathing?

answers.text: Immediately leave the child to call 911 before any CPR is started
Begin 5 cycles of CPR before doing anything else
For a witnessed sudden collapse, leave to activate emergency response and get an AED before starting CPR; for an unwitnessed collapse, perform 2 minutes of CPR before leaving
Stand by and wait for someone else to arrive, since one rescuer is insufficient

explanations.a: The decision depends on whether the collapse was witnessed; AHA does not direct an immediate exit before any CPR for unwitnessed collapses.
explanations.b: Five cycles is the unwitnessed-collapse rule, but not the witnessed-collapse rule.
explanations.c: AHA Part 6 single-rescuer pediatric BLS: witnessed sudden collapse → activate EMS first (likely a cardiac arrhythmia, AED needed); unwitnessed collapse → 2 minutes of CPR first, then leave to call.
explanations.d: A single rescuer can and should provide CPR; waiting compromises the child's survival.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.keyword: AED application pediatric single rescuer pads
questions.text: A single rescuer is performing pediatric CPR on a 4-year-old. The AED arrives via a bystander. According to AHA Part 6, what is the correct sequence with one rescuer?

answers.text: Continue CPR until the AED operates entirely autonomously without rescuer involvement
Stop CPR and move the child to a different room before applying the AED pads
Wait for EMS to arrive before applying any pads
Pause CPR briefly to apply the pediatric AED pads, follow AED prompts (analyze rhythm, deliver shock if advised), then resume CPR immediately starting with compressions

explanations.a: AEDs require user actions — applying pads, pressing analyze/shock — and do not act autonomously.
explanations.b: The AED is brought to the patient; the patient is not relocated.
explanations.c: Public-access AEDs are designed for immediate use; waiting for EMS defeats the purpose.
explanations.d: AHA Part 6: single rescuer applies pads with brief CPR interruption, follows AED prompts, then resumes CPR for 2 minutes after each shock or "no shock advised" before next analysis.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.text: A 2-rescuer team performs CPR on an unresponsive 6-year-old. According to AHA Part 6 2-rescuer pediatric BLS, what compression-to-ventilation ratio applies?

answers.text: 15:2 — 15 compressions followed by 2 breaths per cycle
30:2 — same as adult 2-rescuer CPR for all pediatric patients
5:1 — 5 compressions to 1 breath
10:1 — 10 compressions to 1 breath

explanations.a: AHA Part 6: with 2 rescuers performing pediatric CPR (child or infant), the ratio changes from 30:2 (single rescuer) to 15:2.
explanations.b: Adult ratio is 30:2 in all configurations; pediatric 2-rescuer ratio is 15:2.
explanations.c: A 5:1 ratio is not part of AHA pediatric BLS guidelines.
explanations.d: A 10:1 ratio is not part of AHA pediatric BLS guidelines.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.text: A 3-person rescue team performs pediatric CPR. According to AHA Part 6, how should the team rotate compressions to maintain quality?

answers.text: Compressors should never rotate to maintain consistent technique

Rotate compressors approximately every 2 minutes (about 5 cycles of 30:2 or 10 cycles of 15:2) — fatigue significantly degrades compression quality after that point even when rescuers do not feel tired
Rotate every 30 seconds to keep all rescuers actively involved
Rotate only when the current compressor explicitly requests a switch

explanations.a: Compressor rotation is recommended to preserve compression quality.
explanations.b: AHA Part 6 (and Part 2 for adults): rotate compressors approximately every 2 minutes during each rhythm-check pause; objective compression quality drops within 1–2 minutes even before subjective fatigue.
explanations.c: Every-30-seconds rotation interrupts CPR too frequently and reduces compression fraction.
explanations.d: Subjective fatigue lags objective decline; relying on rescuer self-report reduces compression quality.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.text: Per AHA Part 6, what is the compression-to-ventilation ratio for SINGLE-rescuer pediatric CPR (child or infant)?

answers.text: 30:2 — the same ratio used for single-rescuer adult CPR

explanations.a: 15:2 is the ratio for 2-rescuer pediatric CPR, not single-rescuer.
explanations.b: 5:1 is not an AHA-recommended ratio.
explanations.c: AHA Part 6: single-rescuer pediatric CPR uses 30:2, the same ratio as single-rescuer adult CPR. The ratio changes to 15:2 only with 2 or more rescuers.
explanations.d: 10:1 is not an AHA-recommended ratio.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.keyword: advanced airway pediatric ventilation rate continuous compressions
questions.text: A team is performing CPR on an intubated 5-year-old with an advanced airway in place. According to AHA Part 6, how should compressions and ventilations be coordinated?

answers.text: Continue 15:2 cycles even with the advanced airway in place
Pause compressions every 6 seconds to allow each ventilation
Stop ventilations entirely once an advanced airway is placed
Provide continuous compressions at 100–120/min with 1 breath every 2–3 seconds (20–30 breaths/min) without pausing compressions for breaths

explanations.a: Once an advanced airway is in place, compressions continue uninterrupted while breaths are delivered asynchronously.
explanations.b: Pausing compressions for ventilations is what is being eliminated when an advanced airway is in place.
explanations.c: Ventilations remain critical; only the synchronization changes.
explanations.d: AHA Part 6 (2020 update): with an advanced airway, give 1 breath every 2–3 seconds (20–30 breaths/min) for infants and children — slightly more frequent than the previous 1 every 6 seconds — while compressions continue without pause.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.keyword: infant compression depth 1.5 inches one third
questions.text: According to AHA Part 6, what is the target compression DEPTH for an infant (under 1 year)?

answers.text: About 1.5 inches (4 cm) — approximately one-third of the chest anterior-posterior diameter
About 0.5 inch (1.2 cm) — minimal pressure to avoid injury
About 3 inches (7.6 cm) — same as for an adolescent
About 2 inches (5 cm) — same as for adults

explanations.a: AHA Part 6: infant depth is approximately 1.5 inches (4 cm), or about 1/3 of the AP chest diameter.
explanations.b: Half an inch is far too shallow and would not generate adequate forward blood flow.
explanations.c: 3 inches exceeds the adolescent target and would risk injury in an infant.
explanations.d: 2 inches is the adult depth, not the infant depth.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.keyword: child compression depth 2 inches one third
questions.text: Per AHA Part 6 pediatric guidance, what is the target compression DEPTH for a child (1 year through puberty)?

answers.text: About 1 inch (2.5 cm)
About 2 inches (5 cm) — approximately one-third of the chest anterior-posterior diameter
About 3 inches (7.6 cm)
Compression depth should be matched to the rescuer's strength rather than the child's anatomy

explanations.a: 1 inch is too shallow for a child and would not produce adequate cardiac output.
explanations.b: AHA Part 6: child depth is approximately 2 inches (5 cm), or about 1/3 of the AP chest diameter — the same depth target as adults but with 1/3-AP guidance for younger children.
explanations.c: 3 inches exceeds the child target and risks rib/internal injury.
explanations.d: Depth is anatomically defined by AHA, not adjusted to rescuer preference.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.text: AHA Part 6 specifies the same compression rate target for infants, children, and adults. What is that rate?

answers.text: 60–80 compressions per minute
80–100 compressions per minute
100–120 compressions per minute
140–160 compressions per minute

explanations.a: 60–80 is too slow and reduces cardiac output.
explanations.b: 80–100 is below the AHA target.
explanations.c: AHA Part 2 and Part 6: 100–120/min compression rate applies to infants, children, and adults.
explanations.d: 140–160 exceeds the AHA target; rates faster than 120 reduce diastolic filling and stroke volume.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.keyword: two finger technique single rescuer infant
questions.text: A single rescuer performs CPR on an infant. According to AHA Part 6, which compression technique is preferred for single-rescuer infant CPR?

answers.text: Two-thumb encircling technique with the rescuer's hands wrapping around the infant's chest
Heel-of-one-hand technique used for adults
Two-hands-together overlapping technique
Two-fingers technique — placing two fingers on the breastbone just below the nipple line, compressing about 1.5 inches

explanations.a: Two-thumb encircling is the preferred technique for 2-rescuer infant CPR, not single-rescuer (because the rescuer must also manage the airway and breaths).
explanations.b: Heel-of-one-hand is for children, not infants.
explanations.c: Two-hands-together is for adults, not infants.
explanations.d: AHA Part 6: single-rescuer infant CPR uses two fingers on the lower sternum, just below the nipple line; two-thumb encircling is preferred when ≥2 rescuers are available.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.text: A 2-rescuer team is performing infant CPR. According to AHA Part 6, what is the preferred compression technique and why?

answers.text: Two-thumb encircling — both thumbs on the lower sternum with the rescuer's hands wrapping the infant's chest, because it generates higher compression pressure and more consistent depth than two fingers
Two fingers on the lower sternum — the same as single-rescuer infant CPR
Heel-of-one-hand on the breastbone, like child CPR
Heel of two hands stacked, like adult CPR

explanations.a: AHA Part 6: with 2 rescuers, two-thumb encircling is preferred because it produces more consistent and effective compressions than the two-finger technique.
explanations.b: Two-finger is acceptable only when only one rescuer is available.
explanations.c: One-hand is for children, not infants.
explanations.d: Two-hand is for adults, not infants.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.keyword: rescue breath volume visible chest rise
questions.text: A rescuer is delivering rescue breaths to an unresponsive child during CPR. According to AHA Part 6, how much volume should each rescue breath deliver?

answers.text: As much volume as possible to ensure full lung expansion
Just enough volume to make the chest visibly rise — over approximately 1 second per breath, avoiding excessive volume that increases gastric inflation and intrathoracic pressure
A double-lung volume forced rapidly to overcome airway resistance
A small puff of less than 50 mL to prevent any chest movement

explanations.a: Excessive volume causes gastric inflation, vomiting, and increased intrathoracic pressure that reduces venous return.
explanations.b: AHA Part 6: deliver each breath over about 1 second, with just enough volume to make the chest visibly rise — visible chest rise is the AHA-recommended endpoint.
explanations.c: Forced rapid breaths increase complications without improving oxygenation.
explanations.d: A breath that does not produce visible chest rise is not delivering adequate ventilation.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.text: During pediatric CPR, the rescue breath does not produce visible chest rise. According to AHA Part 6, what is the appropriate corrective action?

answers.text: Deliver a much larger volume forcefully to overcome the obstruction
Skip ventilations entirely and continue compression-only CPR
Reposition the airway (re-perform head-tilt/chin-lift), check for and remove any visible foreign body, and re-attempt the breath; do not attempt blind finger sweeps
Perform 5 abdominal thrusts on the unresponsive child before another breath

explanations.a: Forcing larger volumes does not address airway positioning or obstruction.
explanations.b: Compression-only is inadequate for pediatric arrest because oxygenation is the primary deficit.
explanations.c: AHA Part 6 and Part 11: re-open the airway with head-tilt/chin-lift (or jaw thrust if trauma), remove visible foreign objects, then re-attempt; blind finger sweeps risk pushing objects deeper.
explanations.d: Abdominal thrusts in a known unresponsive arrest patient differ from the FBAO algorithm; reposition the airway first.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.keyword: bag mask E-C clamp visible chest rise
questions.text: A team uses a bag-mask device for ventilation during pediatric CPR. According to AHA Part 6, what is the correct technique to optimize ventilation while minimizing gastric inflation?

answers.text: Squeeze the bag fully and rapidly to deliver maximum volume per breath
Bypass the mask seal and deliver breaths through the bag alone
Hold the breath for 5–10 seconds before releasing
Use a properly sized mask with a tight seal (E–C clamp), squeeze the bag just enough over about 1 second to produce visible chest rise, then release

explanations.a: Rapid full squeezes produce gastric inflation and increase intrathoracic pressure.
explanations.b: A mask seal is essential; without it, ventilation does not reach the lungs.
explanations.c: Holding breaths excessively increases intrathoracic pressure and reduces cardiac output.
explanations.d: AHA Part 6: properly sized mask, E–C clamp seal, gentle squeeze over ~1 second to visible chest rise — minimizes gastric inflation and aspiration risk.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.text: A child has a heart rate of 70 bpm with normal perfusion (warm, pink, alert). According to AHA Part 6, what is the appropriate action?

answers.text: Provide supportive care and monitoring; CPR is NOT initiated because perfusion is adequate at this rate even though it is below normal
Begin CPR immediately because the heart rate is below 100 bpm
Defibrillate at 2 J/kg
Administer naloxone

explanations.a: AHA Part 6: pediatric CPR is initiated when HR < 60 with signs of poor perfusion despite oxygenation and ventilation. A HR of 70 with adequate perfusion does not meet that criterion.
explanations.b: 100 bpm is not the AHA threshold for starting compressions; the threshold is HR < 60 with poor perfusion.
explanations.c: Defibrillation is for shockable rhythms (VF/pulseless VT), not slow heart rate with adequate perfusion.
explanations.d: Naloxone is for suspected opioid overdose, not isolated bradycardia in a perfusing child.

questions.name: Child and Infant CPR
questions.keyword: adult AED for pediatric anterior posterior placement
questions.text: A 5-year-old in cardiac arrest needs defibrillation but only an adult AED with adult pads is available. According to AHA Part 6, what is the appropriate action?

answers.text: Do not use the AED; wait for EMS with pediatric pads

Use the adult AED with adult pads — placing one pad on the chest and one on the back if the pads might touch each other on the small chest — because defibrillation is critical and an adult AED is preferred over no AED
Reduce the AED energy manually before delivery
Use only one of the two pads to avoid the higher energy

explanations.a: Withholding defibrillation costs lives; AHA explicitly endorses adult AED use for pediatric arrest when no pediatric option is available.
explanations.b: AHA Part 6: if pediatric attenuator pads or a pediatric AED are not available, an adult AED with adult pads should be used; place pads anterior-posterior if needed to prevent overlap on a small chest.
explanations.c: AED energy levels are pre-programmed by the device; rescuers cannot manually adjust them.
explanations.d: Both pads are required for the device to deliver a shock and analyze the rhythm.
